composition: Nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%); EDS-measured composition of the 19Al alloy is Fe-41.6, Mn-34.8, Al-18.6, Cu-5.0 (at.%). Within the 15Al/17Al/19Al series the Al variation is achieved by substituting Al for Fe (Fe falls from 44.6 to 41.6 at.%) while Mn (35.2 → 34.8 at.%) and Cu (5.2 → 5.0 at.%) remain essentially constant. Design intent: a high Mn level of ~35 at.% is chosen to promote the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase responsible for the ultra-high, widely tunable hardness; Al is the primary density-reducing element (1 wt.% Al lowers the density by roughly 0.1 g/cm³); Cu was previously shown to accelerate β-Mn precipitation and to raise the hardness of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels. The 19Al alloy has one of the highest Al contents of the family and therefore the lowest density (6.66 g/cm³ by the Archimedes method), at the cost of the slowest β-Mn precipitation kinetics.
conclusions: Within the Fe-35Mn-(15, 17, 19)Al-5Cu low-density steel family the 19Al composition represents the highest-Al, lowest-density end (6.66 g/cm³), in which the α→β-Mn transformation is slowest: the fully transformed β-Mn matrix with fine BCC and FCC Cu-rich interface precipitates obtained after aging at 650 °C for 10 h gives 811.2 ± 19.5 HV, part of an ultra-wide, flexible hardness window of 253.4–965.6 HV that the family can access by simple aging treatments. The study concludes that increasing Al (i) slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn and lengthens the time/temperature needed for complete α→β-Mn transformation, (ii) slightly enhances the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn through solid-solution strengthening, but (iii) decreases the amount of ductile FCC Cu-rich phase between β-Mn interfaces, which lowers both the final hardening effect and the fracture toughness of the ultra-hard alloys (K_IC falling from 8.6 MPa·m¹/² for 15Al to 3.5 MPa·m¹/² for 19Al). The practical implication is that these low-density steels can be shaped in the soft solution-treated state and then aged to a chosen hardness level ("one type of material, multiple uses") at low cost, although the hardness–toughness balance of the high-Al grades still requires further optimization.
mechanisms: α → β-Mn transformation: β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase whose nucleation and growth require long-range atomic diffusion, expelling large amounts of Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix; at aging temperatures of 600 °C and above the driving force for β-Mn formation and the atomic diffusion rate are high enough that the α matrix of the 19Al alloy transforms almost completely into β-Mn within about 1 h, so after 10 h at 650 °C the matrix is essentially fully β-Mn.

Ultra-high hardness originates from the extensive formation of β-Mn: β-Mn has an intrinsic hardness of more than 10 GPa (12.5 ± 0.4 GPa for the β-Mn of the hardest 19Al sample), so the progressive replacement of the soft α matrix by β-Mn produces the rapid, very large aging-hardening response.

Increasing Al content slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn: because β-Mn excludes Al, a higher bulk Al level enriches more Al atoms around the growing β-Mn and hinders its further precipitation and growth, and the Al-rich D0₃ phase (increasingly abundant and stable at high Al content after solution treatment and during aging) must first be depleted before β-Mn can nucleate and grow — this is why the 19Al alloy needs longer times/higher temperatures than 15Al to complete the α→β-Mn transformation.

Formation of the new BCC phase: as β-Mn grows it expels Al to its surroundings, so the Al (a strong BCC stabilizer) enriches at the β-Mn interfaces; this locally stabilizes a new fine BCC phase that precipitates within the β-Mn / at the β-Mn interfaces.

Formation of the FCC Cu-rich phase: Cu has limited solubility in Fe-based alloys and is rejected by the growing β-Mn, so Cu concentrates at the β-Mn interfaces where a fine FCC Cu-rich phase forms; these particles frequently contain FCC twins, and the β-Mn itself is correspondingly Cu-poor.

Hardness of the ultra-hard state depends on both the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn and its absolute volume fraction: increasing Al slightly raises the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn by solid-solution strengthening (Al in β-Mn rising from 14.3 to 17.5 at.% across 15Al→19Al), but it also increases the amount of softer FCC Cu-rich and BCC phases between the β-Mn interfaces, lowering the absolute β-Mn fraction and thus the overall hardness of the highest-Al alloy.

Aging temperature rather than time controls the hardness of the 19Al alloy: once the α→β-Mn transformation is complete (which occurs within ~1 h at 600 °C and above) and the interface precipitates approach saturation, further holding at 650 °C produces almost no hardness change, giving the flat ~801–811 HV plateau of the 650 °C series.
microstructure: In the solution-treated baseline the 19Al alloy is single-phase α (BCC) with a much finer, equiaxed, multi-coloured grain structure than the 15Al and 17Al alloys; no γ (FCC) region is resolved in the phase map. After aging at 650 °C for 10 h the α matrix has almost completely transformed into β-Mn, forming a near-fully transformed matrix of near-equiaxed grains. Numerous fine precipitates are present within the β-Mn and at the β-Mn interfaces: (i) a new BCC phase, appearing as fine dispersed particles within the β-Mn, and (ii) an FCC Cu-rich phase, appearing as fine particles situated at the interfaces between β-Mn grains. The fine interface particles were identified by SAED as having an FCC crystal structure with FCC twins frequently observed inside them; the Cu-rich particles are rich in Cu, depleted in Fe and Mn and slightly poor in Al, whereas the β-Mn is poor in Cu. The phase evolution during aging follows the sequence α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase; for the 19Al alloy aged at ≥600 °C the α matrix is almost completely transformed into β-Mn after just 1 h, and the α→β-Mn transformation of the highest-Al alloy is thermally activated and slow at low temperature (only 12.1 % β-Mn after 525 °C/10 h).
processing: Ingots of nominal Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) were produced by vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h and then hot-rolled into plates 4 mm thick. Plates were cut by electrical discharge machining into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens for Vickers hardness testing and microstructure characterization. Specimens were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon followed by oil quenching — the common baseline state of the alloy, with a hardness of 263.8 ± 1.1 HV. This solution-treated state was then aged at 650 °C for 10 h and water quenched, which is the condition described here. Across the family, aging was performed between 525 °C and 650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h followed by water quenching.
properties: Vickers hardness of the bulk 19Al alloy aged at 650 °C for 10 h and water quenched: 811.2 ± 19.5 HV (HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, 9.8 N load, 15 s dwell, each sample measured 5 times and averaged, 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens). The 650 °C series of the 19Al alloy is essentially time-independent (plateau of ~801–811 HV from 1 h to 10 h), and the 625 °C series plateaus at ~856–871 HV, i.e. for this alloy the aging temperature rather than the aging time dominates the hardness; for comparison the 600 °C series reaches ~895–918 HV and the solution-treated baseline is 263.8 ± 1.1 HV. Specimens for hardness, XRD, SEM and EBSD were prepared by electrolytic polishing in 10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol; TEM foils were mechanically ground to ~90 μm, punched to 3 mm discs and ion thinned. Characterization techniques applied to this alloy family (with this sample characterized by Vickers microhardness, SEM/SE imaging and EBSD) include XRD (D8 Discover), SEM (ZEISS Sigma 300, 5 kV) with SE/EDS, EBSD (GeminiSEM 300, step size 1.5 μm low magnification / 0.05 μm high magnification), TEM/EDS (FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV) and nanoindentation (Agilent G200, 200 nm depth). No tensile, fracture-toughness or physical-property measurements are reported for this specific aging condition.
summary: The "19Al" member of a Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu (at.%, x = 15, 17, 19) family of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels, in the state obtained by solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon + oil quenching and subsequent aging at 650 °C for 10 h followed by water quenching. The parent study asks how Al content controls the aging-hardening behaviour of these steels, which is governed by precipitation of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase. In this sample the α (BCC) matrix has almost completely transformed into near-equiaxed β-Mn, with fine new BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates decorating the β-Mn interfaces, yielding a Vickers hardness of 811.2 ± 19.5 HV.
unmapped: The XRD patterns (Fig. 10) were measured on 15Al at 550 °C/1 h, 17Al at 575 °C/1 h and 19Al at 550 °C/6 h — not on the 19Al 650 °C/10 h condition reported here; they show α/D0₃ together with both α-Mn and β-Mn, indicating that α-Mn and β-Mn co-precipitate before the α matrix fully transforms to β-Mn.

TEM/SAED and EDS elemental mapping (Figs. 11 and 12) were performed on the hardest samples of the family — 15Al at 600 °C/6 h (965.6 HV) and 17Al at 575 °C/6 h (924.9 HV) — and not on the 19Al 650 °C/10 h sample; the FCC-twin-bearing Cu-rich interface particles and the Cu-poor β-Mn were characterized there.

Nanoindentation (Agilent G200, 200 nm depth, 5 μm spacing) and indentation fracture-toughness measurements were made on the peak-hardness samples: 15Al 600 °C/6 h (965.6 HV, K_IC 8.6 MPa·m¹/²), 17Al 575 °C/6 h (924.9 HV, 6.6 MPa·m¹/²) and 19Al 600 °C/10 h (917.8 HV, 3.5 MPa·m¹/²); nanoindentation averages were 11.7 ± 0.4, 11.1 ± 0.6 and 10.4 ± 1.3 GPa respectively, with intrinsic β-Mn hardnesses of 12.1 ± 0.3, 12.2 ± 0.1 and 12.5 ± 0.4 GPa. The 19Al 650 °C/10 h sample was not among the samples tested by nanoindentation.

For the 19Al alloy the EBSD phase-map volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich + BCC precipitates was reported as 6.5 % for the 650 °C/6 h condition (Vickers hardness 810.9 HV), compared with 3.9 % for 15Al at 650 °C/3 h (852.3 HV) and 4.7 % for 17Al at 650 °C/10 h (833.2 HV); the reported 19Al 650 °C/10 h hardness (811.2 ± 19.5 HV) is essentially identical to the 650 °C/6 h value, consistent with the time-independent 650 °C plateau.

Because of the ultra-high hardness, cracks were generated during Vickers indentation; average radial crack lengths were 18 μm (15Al), 22 μm (17Al) and 35 μm (19Al) for the hardest samples, the input for the K_IC calculation using K_IC = 0.016 (E/HV)^1/2 · P/c^(2/3) with E = 164, 175 and 181 GPa for 15Al, 17Al and 19Al.

The 19Al alloy's density (Archimedes, 6.66 g/cm³) and the family's maximum specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g were achieved by the 15Al (Fe-35.2Mn-15Al-5.2Cu) composition, not by the 19Al sample described here.
